result.markdown: --- title: "Interventions and optimization" course-unit: ch15-interventions-and-optimization status: complete --- ## Where we are | Model | Determinism | Time | State | Representation | |---|---|---|---|---| | ODE, function map | deterministic | cont. or discrete | continuous | population | | Markov chain | stochastic | discrete | discrete | population | | Jump process | stochastic | continuous | discrete | population | | SDE | stochastic | continuous | continuous | population | | **Agent-based (next)** | **stochastic** | **discrete** | **discrete** | **individual** | Sensitivity, identifiability, and observation models are questions asked *about* any of these. Today asks what to *do* with one. ::: {.notes} The Day 3 recap slot. Everything so far has been a population model, where the state is counts; the final session fills the individual column, where the state is people. This session moves along a different axis again: not a new model class, but a decision made with a model you already have. ::: ## What this session is for - A tour of what specialised packages add **once a model exists**. - The scenario half is machinery you already have: the Day 1 lockdown callback, reused. A vaccination campaign is the same pattern on a different parameter. - The optimisation half works one small problem end to end, so the *shape* of an optimisation is recognisable when you meet a bigger one. - You leave with pointers, not with a complete treatment of optimal control. ::: {.notes} Say this out loud at the start. The aim is recognition and orientation, not mastery: nobody should feel they are behind because they cannot yet write an optimal-control problem from scratch. Everything in the first half is a callback they have already used; everything in the second half is one worked example plus a reading list. ::: ## Scenario first, optimization second An intervention analysis has two auditable layers: 1. specify a policy and simulate it; 2. compare admissible policies with an explicit objective and constraints. The baseline is the course SIR model. A 50% transmission reduction lasts $d=10$ time units; only its start $t_1\in[0,25]$ is optimized. ::: {.notes} Separating these layers prevents an optimizer from hiding an implementation error or an implicit policy assumption. ::: ## Controlled SIR equations Add cumulative incidence $C$ and a rectangular control: $$ \begin{aligned} \dot S&=-\beta c(1-v(t))SI/N,\\ \dot I&=\beta c(1-v(t))SI/N-\gamma I,\\ \dot R&=\gamma I,\\ \dot C&=\beta c(1-v(t))SI/N, \end{aligned} $$ $$ v(t;t_1)= \begin{cases} v_{\max},&t_1\le t ``` A callback-defined policy compared with no intervention. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} `PresetTimeCallback` changes the parameter at two known times. It implements the scenario; it does not search over policies. ::: ## Bounded timing optimization Four pieces: objective, derivative rule, starting point and box, method. ::: {#cell-ch11-slide-optimize .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#ch11-slide-optimize .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 13.840352420007697 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Read the four pieces aloud in order rather than explaining the algorithm. The finite-difference rule is chosen because each objective evaluation runs a whole ODE solve. `solve` is the same verb as for an ODEProblem: a different problem type selects a different method. ::: ## The grid confirms the optimizer {.center .smaller} ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch11-objective .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch11-objective .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Final cumulative incidence across admissible intervention starts, with the optimizer's answer marked. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} The optimizer returns a continuous timing estimate; the grid shows whether the objective is flat or has several plausible starts. Both are computed here, so the two markers agreeing is the check. ::: ## Validation, interpretation, and limits For every solved policy check $$ \max_t|S(t)+I(t)+R(t)-N|<10^{-6},\qquad \Delta C(t)\ge 0. $$ - The “optimal” result is conditional on reduction, duration, horizon, and cost. - Instantaneous switching, perfect adherence, homogeneous mixing, and a closed population are idealizations. - Add intervention cost, capacity, equity, uncertainty, or a peak-infection penalty when those are decision requirements. **Where to go next** - [Optimization.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/Optimization/stable/): solvers and differentiation backends. - [Parameter estimation](../../chapters/12-parameter-estimation.html): the same problem shape with a likelihood as the objective. - [Advanced optimal control](../../chapters/16-advanced-optimal-control.html): a control function of time, via InfiniteOpt. - [Book chapter](../../chapters/15-interventions-and-optimization.html) and [DiffEqCallbacks.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqCallbacks/stable/). ::: {.notes} The model is useful for learning how to formulate a decision, not for issuing a universal policy recommendation. Advanced continuous controls are deferred to the optimal-control appendix. :::
